(6.4.3 Overbanking

In the locked position the lever is touching one or other of the banking pins.

It may happen that, if the balance is incorrectly placed in the movement, the impulse pin comes into contact with the back of the horn; the movement of the balance will thus be halted (fig. 6-58). In this case the watch will not function, but this problem can be easily solved by positioning the lever against the correct banking pin when the balance is placed in the movement.

It may also happen that a shock shifts the lever from its original position against one or other of the banking pins (fig. 6-59). Such an event tends to cause the lever to come into contact with the other banking pin too early. In this case, and if the guard pin is absent, the impulse pin will not come into contact with the notch but the back of the horn when it completes its

descending supplementary arc. The watch will stop immediately.

This fault is called overbanking. It is the moment when the impulse pin accidentally comes into contact with the back of the horn instead of the fork notch.

Safety devices to avoid overbanking

The guard pin or the extremity of the fork lever formed as a solid guard serves to avoid overbanking _by coming into contact with the rim of the safety er. ‘watch stops with a tooth on the locking plane when the escapement cannot unlock purely through the action of the balance spring.

stopping on the locking plane is most likely when the watch is fully wound (M,,,, ).

et watches and large diameter wristwatches

Pock' (more than ~ 24 mm) should never stop on the locking plane. It cannot be avoided, however, that small-

er watches, fully wound, may stop on the locking plane (fig. 6-60). This should never occur in small watches after they have been running for 24 hours.

Stopping on the impulse plane

A watch is stopped on the impulse plane when it does not start automatically, after unlocking has occurred, while it is being wound (fig. 6-61). A tooth of the escape wheel presses on the impulse plane of one or other of the pallet jewels.

All watches stop on the impulse plane when the mainspring is hardly wound. After having wound the mainspring by 2 or 3 ratchet-wheel teeth a pin or a soft brush is used to move the balance until stopping on the impulse occurs. During the descending supplementary arc of the balance (fig. 6-77), the discharging pallet (E), which forms part of the small roller, comes into contact with a very fine spring (A), generally made of gold, and displaces the detent (B). This in turn causes the locking pallet (C), which forms part of the detent, to unlock the tooth on the escape wheel, allowing the latter to advance one tooth.

Another tooth on the escape wheel drops on to the impulse pallet (D), which forms part of the large roller, and transmits the necessary energy for the balance to make its ascending supplementary arc.

The discharging pallet has now left the gold spring and ceased to displace the detent. The locking pallet regains its original position to lock the next tooth of the escape wheel. The balance continues to turn until it has completed its arc, whereupon it returns.

During the subsequent descending supplementary arc of the balance, the escape wheel is locked. In effect, only the gold spring is lifted when the discharging pallet passes. It then returns immediately to its position against the detent.

This is a recoil escapement which is mainly found in very old pocket watches.

The escape wheel arbor is at 90° to the balance staff (verge). The latter carries two pallets which are separated by a distance corresponding to the escape wheel diameter. The balance staff, with integral pallets, takes the place of separate pallets (fig. 6-81).

As an escape wheel tooth contacts the first pallet, thus providing the necessary impulse for the balance to oscillate, the second pallet contacts the Opposite escape wheel tooth and virtually locks it.

The escape wheel recoils slightly as the balance oscillates, repelled by the second pallet. The recoil ceases as the balance commences its oscillation
